costGuide.title: Volkswagen CNHA Engine Replacement Cost (UK)
costGuide.labourLine: Fitting a CNHA typically takes 8-11 hours at £65/hr (independent specialist rate) - confirm exact labour when comparing quotes.
paragraphs: The replacement cost for a Volkswagen CNHA engine is heavily influenced by the condition of the emissions hardware. Units with a recently serviced AdBlue system (including NOx sensors and the dosing heater) and a professionally cleaned DPF command a premium. Always verify if the EGR cooler has been inspected, as this is a known wear item on higher-mileage examples. failures.title: Volkswagen CNHA Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: AdBlue System Component Failure - 2014-2021 models
items.whatHappens: The CNHA relies heavily on its Selective Catalytic Reduction (SCR) system to meet strict Euro 6 emissions standards. The AdBlue heater element or NOx sensors are prone to failure, triggering dashboard warning lights and potentially putting the vehicle into a reduced-power "limp" mode to prevent excessive emissions.
items.repairVsReplace: This is often resolved by replacing the specific faulty sensor or heater element (£400-£1,500 ). However, if AdBlue crystallisation has damaged the injector or the tank itself, a full system replacement may be required, making a reconditioned Volkswagen CNHA engine a more viable long-term solution.

items.title: DPF Clogging (Urban Use)
items.whatHappens: As an "Ultra" efficiency engine, the CNHA is frequently used for long motorway runs. When subjected to short, urban journeys, the Diesel Particulate Filter (DPF) cannot complete its active regeneration cycle. This leads to soot buildup, restricted exhaust flow, and eventual turbocharger strain due to excessive backpressure.
items.repairVsReplace: A professional DPF clean or forced regeneration can resolve early-stage clogging. If the DPF is physically cracked or the turbo has suffered oil starvation due to the blockage, Volkswagen CNHA engine replacement is often the most reliable fix.

items.title: Occasional EGR Cooler Leaks
items.whatHappens: The Exhaust Gas Recirculation (EGR) cooler can develop internal or external coolant leaks over time. This may present as a sweet smell from the engine bay, unexplained coolant loss, or white smoke from the exhaust under load.
items.repairVsReplace: Replacing the EGR cooler is a standard, manageable repair. It rarely warrants a full Volkswagen CNHA engine replacement unless the leak has been ignored long enough to cause severe hydrolock or overheating damage.

failures.goodYearsLine: The CNHA (part of the broader EA288 family) is generally considered significantly more reliable than its predecessor, the EA189, with far fewer catastrophic timing chain or injector failure issues reported by UK specialists .

variants.title: How to Confirm You Have the CNHA
variants.intro: The CNHA engine code is stamped directly onto the engine block, typically located on a machined pad near the junction of the engine and gearbox, or on a manufacturer sticker affixed to the timing belt cover. It is also clearly listed in your vehicle's V5C registration document under the "Engine Capacity" or "Engine Code" section, and can be definitively verified via a VIN decode. The CNHA is sometimes confused with other EA288 2.0 TDI codes, such as the CRLB or CRBC. While they share the same fundamental architecture, the CNHA is specifically calibrated for "Ultra" low-emission efficiency. This often involves specific AdBlue dosing strategies, unique software maps, and revised exhaust routing. Fitting a non-CNHA replacement may result in ECU incompatibility, failed MOT emissions tests, or incorrect AdBlue consumption rates.

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement CNHA - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: A used Volkswagen CNHA engine can be a cost-effective choice for older, lower-value Golf or Passat hosts, provided the seller can supply documented evidence of regular AdBlue system servicing and DPF regeneration history. The primary risk is inheriting a clogged DPF or a failing NOx sensor that will require immediate attention.

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: This is the recommended route for most CNHA owners. A proper reconditioned unit will have the AdBlue injector, NOx sensors, and EGR cooler rigorously tested or replaced, and the DPF professionally cleaned or renewed. This eliminates the most common failure points and restores the engine to near-factory reliability.

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: A full rebuild is justified for high-mileage Tiguan or Passat examples where the core block is sound, but ancillary components (such as the turbocharger or high-pressure fuel pump) show significant wear. Ensure the rebuild specification explicitly addresses the EA288 emissions hardware to prevent recurring issues.

buyingGuide.supplyFitLine: Booking through our network ensures your CNHA is installed by specialists familiar with VW Group emissions software, backed by a minimum 12-month warranty and nationwide delivery.
buyingGuide.vehicleValueNote: With typical host vehicles (Golf Mk7, Passat B8, Tiguan Mk2) valued between £5,000 and £20,000 , a reconditioned CNHA replacement remains well within the vehicle's value. This makes repair a financially sound decision over scrapping, earning a Safe rating on our ownership decision index.

items.question: How much does a Volkswagen CNHA engine replacement cost?
items.answer: A Volkswagen CNHA engine replacement typically costs between £2,800 and £4,500 for a reconditioned supply-only unit . Fitted costs add approximately £520-£715 for independent specialist labour. Used units are available from £1,200, though they carry higher risk regarding AdBlue and DPF health.

items.question: What is the most common failure with the CNHA 2.0 TDI Ultra?
items.answer: The most documented failure pattern for the CNHA is AdBlue system component failure, typically occurring between 100,000 and 180,000 miles . NOx sensors or the AdBlue heater element frequently fail, triggering limp mode. DPF clogging is also common if the vehicle is primarily used for short, urban journeys.
bullets: NOx sensors or the AdBlue heater element frequently fail, triggering limp mode.
DPF clogging is also common if the vehicle is primarily used for short, urban journeys.

items.question: Which Volkswagen models use the CNHA engine?
items.answer: The CNHA engine was fitted to the Volkswagen Golf (Mk7/Mk7.5), Passat (B8), and Tiguan (Mk2) between 2014 and 2021. It was primarily marketed as the "Ultra" efficiency variant of the 2.0 TDI. It is also shared with select Audi models, including the A4 and A6.

items.question: Should I buy a used or reconditioned CNHA engine?
items.answer: A reconditioned CNHA engine is strongly recommended over a used unit due to the known wear patterns of the EA288 emissions hardware. A proper recon will address or replace the AdBlue injector, NOx sensors, and EGR cooler. Used units often inherit clogged DPFs or failing AdBlue heaters, leading to immediate post-purchase repair bills.
bullets: A proper recon will address or replace the AdBlue injector, NOx sensors, and EGR cooler.

items.question: How do I know if my car has the CNHA engine?
items.answer: You can confirm your vehicle has the CNHA engine by checking the V5C registration document or the manufacturer sticker on the timing belt cover. The code is also stamped on a machined pad near the engine and gearbox junction. Do not confuse it with the CRLB or CRBC, as fitting the wrong revision can cause ECU and emissions incompatibility.
